items.name: Greetings & farewells
items.fushaNote: Most Levantine greetings are MSA-shared (salām, ahlan), but day/night formulas (ṣabāḥ il-khēr / masā il-khēr) and responses (ṣabāḥ in-nūr) are colloquial conventions.

forms.label: reply to ṣabāḥ il-khēr
forms.context: Reply to: ṣabāḥ il-khēr (lit. 'morning of light')

forms.label: reply to masā il-khēr
forms.context: Reply to: masā il-khēr (lit. 'evening of light')

forms.label: reply to ahlan wa-sahlan
forms.context: Reply to: ahlan wa-sahlan / ahlan (warm reply)

items.name: I want X (biddi)
items.fushaNote: From بِودّي ('with my desire'). bidd- + pronoun suffix = 'want'. MSA verb: أريد (urīd). Negation in spoken Levantine: mā bidd- or with -sh: mā biddīsh.

items.name: Can I / could you... (mumkin)
items.fushaNote: ممكن is shared with MSA (literally 'possible'). In spoken use it's a soft modal — 'can I...?', 'could you...?'. Polite and very common.

forms.label: could I... (lit. is it possible I...)

items.name: I have X (ʿindi)
items.fushaNote: ʿind- + pronoun suffix = 'at/with [me]', i.e. 'have'. Same construction as MSA. Negation: mā ʿind-. The ʿ is the voiced pharyngeal — don't drop it.

items.name: I go / present tense (b- prefix) — rāḥ
items.fushaNote: Levantine present-habitual / general present takes b- prefix on the imperfect: barūḥ = 'I go / I'm going'. Without b-, the bare imperfect is used after modals (biddi arūḥ). MSA: أذهب (aḏhab).

items.name: I went / past tense — rāḥ
items.fushaNote: Past tense in Levantine takes the same suffix paradigm as MSA, with some pronunciation shifts (e.g. 1sg/2sg.m collapse: ruḥt). MSA: ذهبتُ (ḏahabtu).

items.name: I will go / future (raḥ + verb)
items.fushaNote: Levantine future marker is رح (raḥ), originally from رايح ('going'). It precedes the bare imperfect (no b- prefix). MSA: سـ / سوف.

items.name: Do this / don't do this (imperative)
items.fushaNote: Levantine imperative drops MSA's initial hamza in many cases (kul not ʾukul). Negative imperative = lā + 2nd-person bare imperfect: lā tākul = 'don't eat'.

forms.label: wait! (m)
forms.context: Said to a man. Verb istanna ('to wait'); noun: intiẓār ('waiting').

forms.label: repeat! (m)
forms.context: Said to a man. Verb aʿād / yʿīd ('to repeat / do again', Form IV); noun: iʿāda ('a repetition').

forms.label: slow down (m)
forms.context: Lit. 'on your leisure / at your own pace'. Said to a man; to a woman: ʿala mahlik.

items.name: Question words (shū, wēn, ēmta, lēsh, kīf, ʾaddēsh)
items.fushaNote: Levantine has its own question words diverging from MSA: شو (shū) ← MSA ما/ماذا; وين (wēn) ← MSA أين; ليش (lēsh) ← MSA لماذا; إيمتى (ēmta) ← MSA متى; قدّيش (ʾaddēsh) is dialectal for 'how much/how many'.

items.name: I like / love (baḥebb, biʿjibni)
items.fushaNote: بحبّ (baḥebb) = 'I like / love' — same root as MSA أحبّ. The construction [thing] + biʿjibni (literally 'pleases me') is very common for 'I like [thing]', parallel to Spanish 'me gusta'.

forms.label: it (m) pleases me
forms.context: About a masculine-gender thing (lit. 'it pleases me')

forms.label: it (f) pleases me
forms.context: About a feminine-gender thing (lit. 'it pleases me')

items.name: I have to / need to (lāzim)
items.fushaNote: لازم (lāzim) is invariable in spoken Levantine — 'must / have to / should'. The verb following is the bare imperfect (no b-). Negation: mish lāzim ('don't have to / not necessary'). MSA equivalent: يجب أن (yajib an).

items.name: Numbers 1–1000 + ordinals (with counter)
items.fushaNote: Spoken Levantine numbers 1–10 mostly match MSA with phonetic shifts. Numbers 11–19 have a distinctive -ṭaʿsh ending (← MSA -ʿashar). Tens 20–90 take a uniform -īn suffix. Counter rules: shēʾel (sg) for 1 and 11+; shawāʾil (pl) for 3–10. Compounds put the unit first, then w- ('and'), then the ten: wāḥad w-ʿishrīn = 21 (lit. 'one and twenty').

forms.label: twenty-one
forms.context: Lit. 'one and twenty'. All compound numbers 21-99 follow this pattern: unit + w- + ten.

forms.label: one hundred
forms.context: Spelled مية or مائة. Hundreds 200-900 combine miyye with a number in the construct form (no -e/-a ending): khams miyye = 500, miyyatēn = 200 (dual).

forms.label: first
forms.context: Feminine: ūla (e.g. il-mara l-ūla = the first time). Also functions as 'beginning of' in iḍāfa: awwal shāriʿ = (the) first street.

forms.label: second
forms.context: Feminine: tānye. Also means 'other / another' (shi tāni = something else).

items.name: Colours (with m / f forms)
items.fushaNote: The six 'classical' colours (white, black, red, green, blue, yellow) follow the af3al / fa3la pattern: masculine starts with a- (aḥmar, akhḍar), feminine drops the initial a- and reshapes the vowels (ḥamra, khaḍra). Newer / loan colours (bunni, rmādi) don't inflect this way — same form for both genders.

forms.label: white (f)
forms.context: Feminine — used with feminine nouns: sayyāra bēḍa (a white car).

forms.label: black (f)
forms.context: Feminine — ʾahwe sōda = black coffee (i.e. without milk).

forms.label: red (f)
forms.context: Feminine — il-ishāra l-ḥamra = the red light.

forms.label: green (f)
forms.context: Feminine. Also a common woman's name.

forms.label: blue (m)
forms.context: Everyday qāf glottalises here: azraʾ. (Formal / written: azraq.)

forms.label: brown
forms.context: Doesn't inflect strongly by gender — bunni works for both, though some speakers use bunniyye for feminine nouns.

forms.label: grey
forms.context: Lit. 'ash-colour' — from rmād ('ash'). Same form for both genders.

forms.label: light (modifier)
forms.context: Modifier — comes AFTER the colour: aḥmar fātiḥ = light red, azraʾ fātiḥ = light blue.

forms.label: dark (modifier)
forms.context: Modifier — comes AFTER the colour: aḥmar ghāmiʾ = dark red. The qāf glottalises: ghāmiʾ.

items.name: Time markers (yesterday, today, tomorrow, now)
items.fushaNote: Levantine time words: hallaʾ (now) ← MSA al-ʾān; mbāriḥ (yesterday) ← MSA al-bāriḥa; bukra (tomorrow) ← MSA ghadan. il-yōm (today) is shared with MSA but pronounced with the ō diphthong-shift.

items.name: Connectors (that, so, when, because, if, …)
items.fushaNote: These small words do most of the heavy lifting for stringing thoughts together in Levantine. The relative pronoun illi covers all of MSA's allaḏī / allatī / allaḏīna (gender + number distinctions are dropped). The complementizer inno covers MSA anna / inna. Conditionals split: iza for real conditions ('if it rains'), law for unreal / hypothetical or polite ('if you would'). And yaʿni functions as 'I mean', 'so', and a filler all at once — you'll hear it in almost every sentence.

forms.label: that / which / who (relative)
forms.context: Used to introduce a relative clause: il-walad illi hōn = 'the boy who('s) here'; ish-shi illi biddi = 'the thing that I want'. No gender/number agreement — one form covers all.

forms.label: that (complementizer)
forms.context: Used after verbs of thinking, saying, knowing: baʿtaʾid inno jāy = 'I think (that) he's coming'; ʾāl inno mā byaʿrif = 'he said (that) he doesn't know'.

forms.label: when (subordinator)
forms.context: Introduces a time clause: lamma ruḥt ʿa s-sūʾ = 'when I went to the market'. Distinct from ēmta? ('when?', the question word).

forms.label: because
forms.context: la- ('for / because') + anno ('that'). la-anno bardān = 'because (it's) cold'. Variant: li-anno.

forms.label: if (real condition)
forms.context: Used for real / possible conditions: iza biddak, fīna nrūḥ = 'if you want, we can go'. For unreal / hypothetical or politeness, use law (as in law samaḥt 'if you would').

forms.label: so / therefore
forms.context: Lit. 'for this' — la- ('for') + hēk ('this'). kān bardān, la-hēk libist jakēt = 'it was cold, so I wore a jacket'.

forms.label: I mean / so
forms.context: Lit. 'it means' (from MSA يعني). Ubiquitous filler / discourse marker: 'so, basically, you know'. yaʿni shū? = 'so what?' / 'meaning?'. Also literal: hāda yaʿni ʾahwe = 'this means coffee'.

forms.label: or (in questions)
forms.context: The everyday spoken 'or' in either/or questions: shāy willā ʾahwe? = 'tea or coffee?'. Etymologically 'and-not'.

forms.label: or (formal / either … or)
forms.context: More formal or written 'or'. willā is more common in spoken use; aw shows up in lists and writing: aḥmar aw azraʾ = 'red or blue'.

forms.label: even
forms.context: ḥatta huwwe mā byaʿrif = 'even he doesn't know'. Also means 'until' in time expressions: ḥatta bukra = 'until tomorrow'.

forms.label: maybe
forms.context: yimken bukra = 'maybe tomorrow'. Lit. 'it is possible'. Variant: balki (more colloquial, leans 'perhaps').

forms.label: of course
forms.context: Lit. 'naturally' (from ṭabʿ, 'nature'). Used to agree warmly: ṭabʿan! = 'of course!'.

items.name: This / that — pointing & equational sentences
items.fushaNote: Levantine demonstratives are reduced from MSA: hāda ← hāḏā, hāy/hādi ← hāḏihi, hadōl ← hāʾulāʾ, hadāk ← ḏālika, hadīk ← tilka. Equational sentences need no copula: 'hāda kitāb' = 'this is a book'. Negation uses mish before the predicate.

forms.label: this (m)
forms.context: Pointing at a masculine noun (kitāb, walad, bēt...)

forms.label: this (f)
forms.context: Pointing at a feminine noun (sayyāra, sāʿa, binit...)
forms.pronunciationNote: Also said hādi; hāy is the more common short form in Palestinian.

forms.label: these
forms.context: Pointing at a plural noun (any gender)

forms.label: that (m, distal)
forms.context: Pointing further away — 'that one over there'

items.name: My / your / his / her — possessive suffixes
items.fushaNote: Same suffix system as MSA, with Levantine vowel adjustments: -i, -ak, -ik, -o (← MSA -hu), -ha, -na, -kum, -hum. Joined directly to the noun, no space. Final tāʾ marbūṭa surfaces as -t- before a suffix (sayyāra → sayyārti).

forms.label: my car
forms.context: Note tāʾ marbūṭa → -t- before the suffix

items.name: Whose? / mine, yours, his (independent possessives)
items.fushaNote: Levantine has two parallel independent possessive sets: تبع (taʿ-) and إل (il-). Both attach the same pronoun suffixes used on nouns. taʿ- is more pan-Levantine; ilī/ilak/etc. is also frequent, especially in shorter answers ('ilī' = 'mine'). MSA uses لـ (li-) similarly.

forms.label: whose is this? (with taʿ)
forms.pronunciationNote: taʿ = 'belonging to'; very common spoken alternative to la-mīn.

forms.label: mine
forms.pronunciationNote: Also taʿi. Both common; ilī is shorter, often used as a one-word answer.

forms.label: is this yours? (m)
forms.context: Asking a man about a masculine thing

forms.label: is this yours? (f)
forms.context: Asking a woman about a masculine thing

items.name: There is / there isn't (fī / mā fī)
items.fushaNote: Levantine uses في (fī) as an existential 'there is/are' — distinct from the MSA preposition fī ('in'). Negation is mā fī. Past: kān fī / mā kān fī. MSA equivalent: يوجد (yūjad) / لا يوجد (lā yūjad).

items.name: Give me / I gave (aʿṭa)
items.fushaNote: Levantine 'give' is from MSA أعطى (aʿṭā). The imperative + 1sg object pronoun fuses: aʿṭi + ni → aʿṭīni. Past stem: aʿṭē- (1sg/2sg), aʿṭā- (3sg.m).

forms.label: give me one
forms.context: wāḥad for masculine items; waḥde for feminine items.

forms.label: I gave it (m)
forms.english: I gave it / I gave him.

forms.label: I'll give you (m)
forms.context: b- prefix on the imperfect = habitual / immediate-future 'I give'.

items.name: Bring me X (jīb / jībli)
items.fushaNote: Levantine jāb / yjīb (root j-y-b) replaces MSA أحضر (ʾaḥḍara) / أتى بـ (ʾatā bi-). The imperative + -li ('to me') contracts: jīb + li → jībli (m), jībi + li → jībīli (f), jību + li → jībūli (pl).

items.name: Put it here / on the (ḥaṭṭ)
items.fushaNote: Levantine ḥaṭṭ / yḥuṭṭ (root ḥ-ṭ-ṭ) replaces MSA وضع (waḍaʿa). Imperative ḥuṭṭ (m), ḥuṭṭi (f), ḥuṭṭu (pl). Object pronouns clitic onto the verb: ḥuṭṭ + o → ḥuṭṭo ('put it'-m), + ha → ḥuṭṭha ('put it'-f).

forms.label: I'll put it here
forms.context: b- prefix on the imperfect = immediate-future / habitual.

forms.label: I put it here (already)
forms.context: Past tense — referring to an earlier action.

forms.label: can you put it here?
forms.context: Said to a man. To a woman: mumkin tḥuṭṭīh hōn?

items.name: I learned / past tense — taʿallam
items.fushaNote: taʿallam (Form V, تعلّم) is a regular verb that shows the standard Levantine past-tense suffix paradigm without the stem changes hollow verbs like rāḥ have. Use this engine to internalise the suffixes (-t, -ti, -∅, -at, -na, -tu, -u). MSA: تعلّمتُ (taʿallamtu).

forms.label: you learned (m)
forms.context: Said to a man (same form as 1sg — context distinguishes).

forms.label: where did you learn? (m)
forms.context: To a man. To a woman: wēn tʿallamti?
